strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: improving MLLM compositionality and data efficiency during visual instruction tuning, rather than merely scaling VIT data volume.
COMPACT is simple and intuitive: define atomic visual capabilities, generate capability-composed QA pairs, verify them, and mix them with a small VIT subset to preserve instruction following.
The empirical section is reasonably broad, covering several standard multimodal benchmarks and comparing against full LLaVA-665K, random equal-budget subsets, and ICONS.
The ablations are useful: data scale, balanced vs. unbalanced compositional complexity, capability leave-one-out, complexity range, and VIT mixing ratio all support the core design choices.

The reported data efficiency is promising: with roughly 10% of the LLaVA-665K data budget, COMPACT reaches comparable average performance and improves on some complex-task slices such as MM-Vet and MMStar high-k examples.
weaknesses: The central compositionality claims rely heavily on Gemini for generation, verification, and post-hoc capability annotation of benchmarks. Without human validation or an independent labeling study, the definition of k and the correctness of generated samples are not fully trustworthy.

The evaluation is limited to one model family and setup, LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA. It is unclear whether the recipe transfers to stronger recent MLLMs, different vision encoders, larger models, or full fine-tuning settings.

The main quantitative claim is somewhat overstated: COMPACT is essentially at parity on the aggregate relative score and is worse than full LLaVA-665K on several benchmarks, including MME, TextVQA, CV-Bench, and LLaVA-W.

There are no confidence intervals, multiple random seeds, or repeated subset samples. Several reported gains are small enough that robustness is uncertain, especially for high-k benchmark slices that may contain very few examples.

The baselines are incomplete. The paper should compare against unconstrained Gemini-generated VQA data, other synthetic VIT recipes, k-matched but not capability-balanced data, and stronger data selection or data curation methods beyond ICONS.
The data-efficiency framing counts only training examples and does not account for the cost and reproducibility burden of using a closed-source VLM to generate and verify the compositional data.

The taxonomy of atomic capabilities is somewhat ad hoc and overlapping, and some qualitative examples appear ambiguously labeled, which weakens the claim that the method precisely controls compositional complexity.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: prompts are provided, but the dataset is not yet released in the submission, generation failure rates and filtering statistics are limited, and closed-source Gemini behavior may change over time.
